title: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Summary, May 2026 (JOLTS)
date_evidence: For release 10:00 a.m. (ET) Tuesday, June 30, 2026      USDL-26-1123
key_claim: In May 2026 US hires were unchanged at 5.2 million (a 3.3 percent rate), quits changed little at 3.1 million (1.9 percent rate), layoffs stayed at 1.7 million, and job openings held at 7.6 million: a low-hire, low-fire market with little churn.
frame_summary: The JOLTS release presents a labour market in stasis, with openings, hires, quits and layoffs all essentially unchanged and turnover stuck at low rates.
verbatim_quote: In May, the number of quits changed little at 3.1 million, while the rate was unchanged at 1.9 percent.

title: The Employment Situation, June 2026
date_evidence: Transmission of material in this news release is embargoed until ... 8:30 a.m. (ET) Thursday, July 2, 2026
key_claim: Nonfarm payrolls rose just 57,000 in June, near the 36,000 average monthly gain of the prior 12 months; the long-term unemployed rose 286,000 over the year to 27.3 percent of all unemployed, showing how hard re-entry has become in a low-hiring market.
frame_summary: The release describes an economy still adding some jobs but at a weak pace, with unemployment stable yet increasingly long-duration for those already out of work.
verbatim_quote: Total nonfarm payroll employment changed little in June (+57,000), roughly in line with the average monthly change over the prior 12 months (+36,000).
verbatim_list: The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) changed little at 1.9 million in June but is up by 286,000 over the year. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.3 percent of all unemployed people in June.

title: ADP National Employment Report: Private Sector Employment Increased by 98,000 Jobs in June; Annual Pay was Up 4.4%
key_claim: In June 2026 median pay growth was 4.4 percent for job-stayers while job-changer pay growth accelerated to 6.6 percent: a historically thin switching premium, though one that widened slightly on the month.
frame_summary: ADP presents a slowing but not collapsing labour market in which hiring is uneven, job creation is decelerating, and the job-changer pay advantage remains modest.
verbatim_quote: The median pay gain for job-stayers was little changed at 4.4 percent, while year-over-year pay growth for job-changers accelerated to 6.6 percent.

title: Should I stay or should I go? The pay tradeoff
key_claim: Bank of America internal deposit data show more than 40% of workers seeing flat or declining after-tax pay, the top 5% of earners rewarded most for staying put, and a job-switching premium that persists for the young but has narrowed alongside the broader slowdown.
frame_summary: The Institute argues the labour market may be gradually improving from a frozen state, but that pay progression has stalled for a large share of workers and loyalty now pays best at the top.
verbatim_quote: more than 40% of workers are seeing flat or declining pay after taxes and benefits
verbatim_list: Millennials who moved to another company saw after-tax wages grow twice as fast compared to those who stood still, while the rate of earnings growth increased fourfold for Gen Z.
Payroll growth has picked up and job switching has edged higher, signaling some recovery in Q1 2026.
the top 5% of earners are rewarded far more for their loyalty than any other groups

title: As loyal Boomers win and job-switching Gen Zers lose, the labor market of 2026 reveals a decade of bad career advice
key_claim: The switcher-stayer wage gap fell to 3 points in Q1 2026 (8% vs 5%), the smallest in seven years and down from nearly 11 points in 2022; ADP-tracked data put the premium at a record-low 1.9 percentage points in early 2026; the average new hire is 42 and Gen Z's share of new hires has collapsed.
frame_summary: Fortune argues the decade-old job-hopping playbook has broken in a low-hire, low-fire market that now rewards tenure and experience, squeezing younger workers out of entry and mobility gains.
verbatim_quote: Job switchers saw their after-tax wages grow just 8% year-over-year in Q1 2026, compared to 5% for workers who stayed put. That 3-point gap is the smallest it has been in seven years.
verbatim_list: At the peak of the Great Resignation in 2022, that same gap was nearly 11 points, with switchers pulling almost 18% wage growth while stayers settled for 7%.
shows the switching premium hit a record low of just 1.9 percentage points in early 2026
The average age of a new hire hit 42 in 2025, up from 40.5 in 2022 and 40 in 2016
Revelio Labs finds that Gen Z's share of new hires collapsed from 14.9% to 8.8% between 2022 and 2025, with hiring inflows for workers under 25 down 45% since 2019.

title: Apollo chief economist says there's 'zero evidence' AI is killing jobs; in fact, he says it's creating them
key_claim: Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok argues there is zero evidence of AI-driven job losses and that AI spending is stoking employment, while OpenAI's Sam Altman concedes some 'AI washing' in which companies blame AI for layoffs they would have made anyway.
frame_summary: The piece assembles the sceptical case on AI displacement: prominent economists see no aggregate AI job-loss signal and attribute headline layoffs to other business motives dressed up as AI.

verbatim_list: there's some AI washing where people are blaming AI for layoffs that they would otherwise do, and then there's some real displacement by AI of different kinds of jobs
